name: The Lasipalatsi Willow
age_estimate: about 15 years (the living tree); continuously cultivated at this spot since 1830
access: Free, standing on a public pedestrian street beside the Lasipalatsi building. No restrictions.
story:
The first tree in Finland ever placed under official protection was this one, in 1924, and the protection did not save it. The willow had gone in around 1830 beside the Turku Barracks then being built in Kamppi, grew into one of the best known trees in Helsinki, and came down in a storm on 29 December 2003 after 173 years.

What stands on Salomonkatu today is not that tree. Cuttings had been taken while the old willow was still up, one was raised on, and on 13 April 2011 it went back into the exact spot behind a low protective fence. Genetically it is the same willow, a clone of the 1830 tree. Physically it is about fifteen years old and slight enough that nobody has recorded a girth for it. The address is nearly two centuries old and the trunk is not, and both of those are true at once.

Even the species is unsettled. It is a hybrid weeping willow, isoriippasalava, carrying the cultivar name 'Lasipalatski' after the building beside it, with white willow, weeping willow and Caucasian willow all put forward among its parents.

Two minutes from Kamppi metro, on an open pedestrian street. Travelling to see a young tree sounds like a poor trade until you understand what the spot is, and that the city thought the line worth keeping going.

name: The Independence Spruce
access: Free, standing in the public Kaivopuisto park, north side of the Kaivohuone restaurant. No restrictions.
transport: Tram 3 or bus to Kaivopuisto, 5-10 minute walk into the park
story:
This spruce is exactly as old as the country it stands in. Consul General Rudolf Ray sowed the seed on 6 December 1917, the day the Finnish Parliament accepted the declaration of independence, and then raised the seedling privately for the next thirteen years. After he died in 1930 it was lifted, moved to Kaivopuisto and formally presented to Parliament on 13 May 1931 with full ceremony. A granite stone at its roots carries an alternative design for the national coat of arms, drawn by Ray himself.

Twenty-seven years in, the war reached it. The bombing raids on Helsinki in February 1944 sent shrapnel into the trunk and broke the crown clean off. The tree regrew, slowly enough that by the early 1960s the city's foresters were expecting to lose it to stunted growth. They did not. It stands north of the Kaivohuone restaurant on Iso Puistotie, in a park that walks past it all summer without looking up.

What it does not have is a measurement. No girth, no height, nothing published, which is an odd gap for a tree with a memorial stone and a parliamentary dedication. If you go with a tape measure, tell us what you get.

name: Kalm's Oak
age_estimate: about 275 years (grown from a seed around 1750)

location.address: Sibelius Museum grounds, Piispankatu 17, Turku, on the bank of the Aura river

access: Free. Visible from the public Aura riverside path; the Sibelius Museum's own garden is ticketed and the exact boundary between the two is not signposted.
transport: Central Turku, short walk from the Market Square along the Aura riverside promenade
story:
The Great Fire of Turku in 1827 took most of the city and it took the botanical garden this oak was planted in. The oak is still standing. It grew from a seed around 1750 and went into the ground on the Piispantalo property in the 1760s, part of the garden Pehr Kalm laid out and directed from 1757. Kalm was the Turku Academy's first professor of economics and a student of Linnaeus, and this tree is effectively the last of his garden.

The city's own tree inventory calls it the oldest tree in Turku. Its surveyors measured it on 10 July 2020 and recorded 4.97 metres round and 17 metres tall, on the bank of the Aura between the river and the Sibelius Museum. In 2012 an environmental artwork called Pehr Kalm Revival was installed near it, tracing the plan of the garden that no longer exists.

Approach from the riverside promenade, a short walk from the Market Square. The tree is clearly visible from the public path and that costs nothing. How close you can actually get depends on where the museum's own garden begins, and that boundary is one we have not established. If you walk it and find out, tell us.

name: Paavola's Oak

location.address: Paavola nature trail, Lohjansaari, Lohja (start from the old Lohjansaari school car park, Pietiläntie 23)

access: Free. Stands beside a clearly marked 1 to 1.5km nature trail with 15 information posts inside the Paavolan tammikko nature reserve (protected 1994); a picnic table sits near the tree. Parking at Pietiläntie 23 (about 700m walk to the tree). Part of the surrounding grove is on private land per the reserve's own description, but the tree and the marked trail past it are open to the public.
transport: No public transport to the trailhead; roughly 45 to 60 minutes by car from Helsinki (about 58km), or Lohja town by train/bus then a local taxi/car to Lohjansaari
story:
Finns call this the most beautiful tree in the country, and they were saying so a century before the internet agreed. The photographer and explorer I.K. Inha documented the oak over a hundred years ago, the magazine Tiede ja elämä wrote it up in 1920, and in autumn 2014 a piece by Antti Huttunen for Yle sent it round the country again to an audience that had never heard of it.

The trunk runs to about 4.7 metres round. The reserve's own signage puts the age at 300 to 400 years, which is an estimate rather than a ring count, so the range stays as wide as the sign leaves it. The tree is a protected natural monument, and the grove around it, Paavolan tammikko on Lohjansaari, has been a nature reserve since 1994 for its herb-rich forest floor.

Getting there is half of it. A marked trail of a kilometre or so leaves the old Lohjansaari school car park at Pietiläntie 23, with fifteen information posts along the way and a picnic table near the oak. Part of the surrounding grove is private land; the trail and the tree are the public part. A second protected oak, designated in 1990, stands along the same path, so the walk pays twice.

Roughly an hour by car from Helsinki and no bus to the trailhead. Bring lunch and plan on the afternoon.
container: new single-tree place 'Lohja' per the 2026-08-31 exception (Lohja has no published city page; ~58km from Helsinki, beyond the ~30km day-trip join threshold). Highest-demand candidate in the batch; a named, century-documented, virally famous single oak with its own marked nature trail built to visit it. A second protected oak on the same trail is a future Lohja lead.
